title: Bash exercise
text:
Manipulating sequence data
The “SARS-CoV-2.fasta” file contains nucleotide sequence data from different strains of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The sequences are in a format called FASTA. The FASTA format looks like:
>Name1
AATCGGCTA
>Name2
ATTCGCCTA

Question 2
Use the command line to determine the number of sequences in the “SARS-CoV-2.fasta” file.

Notice all sequences start with a “>” character to specify the seqence’s name. We can use that to count the sequences efficiently. Try:


Bash command line

grep ">" SARS-CoV-2.fasta

NOTE: Putting quotes around the > character is important, because in the Bash language, this character is normally used to redirect output!
grep is a very useful command for finding string patterns. You can learn more about it with man grep.
grep works okay for this small FASTA file, but what if there were 1000s of sequences in the file? You wouldn’t want to count them “by hand!”
We can use the wc command (word count) for counting the sequences. Try:


Bash command line

grep ">" SARS-CoV-2.fasta | wc -l

The pipe (|) character converts, or “pipes”, the output of one command to input to another command. wc -l will count the number of lines output by grep

Put the number of sequences into Question 2 of the Exercise 2 quiz on Canvas.


Question 3
What does the -l flag in the wc -l do? Hint: use the man command to find out!


Question 4
What is your output for the following command?


Bash command line

whoami



Question 5
What is your output for the following command?


Bash command line

echo $MACHTYPE



Question 6
What is your output for the following command?


Bash command line

uname -a



Question 7
What does the -a flag do in the uname -a command (use man to find out!)?

title: Why Computation?
text:
Origins of Comp Bio




1952: Fred Sanger sequenced first protein (insulin)
Margaret Dayhoff & colleagues stored protein sequences in the Protein Information Resource (1960s & 70s)
1960s: Dayhoff & others use computers to infer phylogenies







Margaret Dayhoff







McLaughlin & Dayhoff 19731




McLaughlin and Dayhoff (1973)

title: Why Computation?
text:
Biology became a data science

One human genome: ~3.1 billion base pairs
One NovaSeq run: tens of billions of reads
GenBank, SRA, UniProt, PDB: petabytes, doubling every couple of years
Sequencing costs have fallen faster than computing has gotten cheaper





The bottleneck in modern biology is rarely generating data. It is deciding what to do with it.




Ask: how long would it take to read 3 billion characters at 200 words/min? Roughly 100+ years without sleeping. This is not a “work harder” problem.

title: Why Computation?
text:
The takeaway

A biological question becomes a computational question when we have to specify exactly how to get from data to answer.

What is Python?

title: Why Computation?
text:
What is a Python notebook?

An interactive web-based document that allows you to combine runnable Python code, formatted text, and visualizations in one place.
Composed of modular building blocks called “cells”

Instead of running a whole script of Python code, snippets of code in each cell run individually

title: Why Computation?
text:
Types of cells

Code (Python) cells

Snippets of Python code that run individually; output of code appears underneath the cell

Markdown cells:

Formatted text and images created using Markdown syntax; used to explain/document the code

title: Why Computation?
text:

One type of Python notebook
Jupyter is another type that is more popular

title: Why Computation?
text:
Why marimo?
IMHO, marimo solved two big problems with other types of notebooks:

Results can vary depending on the order cells are run

marimo solves this by being “reactive”

The plain text files of other notebooks are illegible (nested in JSON syntax)

marimo is pure Python

A free, cloud-hosted workspace for running marimo Python notebooks
The name is a play on Google colab, a popular service for Jypyter notebooks
It will be our primary means of practicing comp bio

title: AU COSAM Linux ThinLinc
text:
The IT group of the Collage of Sciences & Mathematics (COSAM IT) hosts a Linux desktop environment that can be run in a web browser using the software called ThinLinc. COSAM IT was kind enough to provide access to this Linux ThinLinc environment to all the students in our class.
Important! Please read the next 2 sections and don’t skip to logging in!

title: AU COSAM Linux ThinLinc
section: Logging out of a ThinLinc session
text:
Logging out of a ThinLinc session
Before we learn how to log in to a ThinLinc session, you need to know how to log out.
You cannot log out by closing your browser window!
Instead you need to:

Click the power icon a the top right of the Linux desktop in your browser window
Click “Power Off/Log Out”
Click “Log Out”







Figure 1: How to log out of a Linux ThinLinc session.



If you do close your brower by mistake, it’s OK! Just go back to https://csm-earth.auburn.edu. The screen might look black, but that is just the Linux desktop’s lock screen. Click the black screen and you will be prompted to enter your password to unlock the screen. Use the same AU password as when you logged in (see below).
If you close your browser without logging out, your ThinLinc session remains active and uses resources on COSAM’s servers. So, please remember to log out when you’re done.

title: AU COSAM Linux ThinLinc
section: I was using ThinLinc but now have a black screen!
text:
I was using ThinLinc but now have a black screen!
No worries, the black screen is the Linux desktop’s lock screen. Click on it and you will be asked to enter your password to unlock the screen. Use the same AU password as when you logged in.

title: AU COSAM Linux ThinLinc
section: Logging in to a ThinLinc session
text:
Logging in to a ThinLinc session

Make sure you are connected to AU’s VPN.
Open your web browser and go to https://csm-earth.auburn.edu. You should see a login screen that looks like the screenshot below.






Figure 2: Linux ThinLinc log in page.



In the “Username” field, enter your AU username (the first part of your AU email before the “@” symbol). For the password, enter the password for you AU account. Then, click “Log in”
You will see a prompt for 2-factor authentication like the one below. Enter the number associated with your preferred mode of authentication. In the example below, to use DUO, type “1” and click “Next.”






Figure 3: Linux ThinLinc prompt for 2-factor authentication.



After authenticating, the Linux Desktop will begin to load in your browser. This can take 30 seconds or so. Once the Linux Desktop has loaded, you can click “Activities” in the upper left of the desktop to reveal a dock along the bottom of the desktop. You can use the dock to launch applications (Figure 4).






Figure 4: How to view the dock and launch apps.

title: AU COSAM Linux ThinLinc
section: Setting up our shared folder in ThinLinc
text:
Setting up our shared folder in ThinLinc
COSAM IT has created a shared folder we can all access within our ThinLinc environment. To set up the shared folder, follow these steps. You only need to do this once!

Click “Activities” in the upper left of the desktop.
From the dock along the bottom, open the “Files” application (its icon is a filing cabinet; see Figure 4)
Along the left of the Files window, click “+ Other Locations”
Along the bottom of the window you will see “Connect to Server” and “Enter server address…” In the “Enter server address…” field type (or copy and paste):
smb://auo11.auburn.edu/csm
and then click “Connect”
Along the left of the you shoud now see “csm on auo11.auburn.edu”. Click on that and then the “Academic - Class Resources” folder
Within the “Academic - Class Resources” folder, you should now see the “Biol5800-6800” folder. Click and drag the “Biol5800-6800” folder to the left of the window, and drop it where you see “New bookmark”.

You can now access the “Biol5800-6800” folder via the “Files” app whenever you are logged into ThinLinc. The whole class has access to this folder, and this is where I will put any files you need to use within the ThinLinc Linux environment.
